slides.heading: Count Squares
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Hard · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Count Squares, a hard arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Number of squares (any orientation) whose four corners are all in the point set.
For each pair as a diagonal, compute the other two corners; each square is found twice.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Number of squares (any orientation) whose four corners are all in the point set. For each pair as a diagonal, compute the other two corners; each square is found twice.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Any two points can be a square's diagonal; the other two corners are then fixed, so just check they exist.
slides.narration: Any two points can be a square's diagonal; the other two corners are then fixed, so just check they exist.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Pairs as diagonals + hash set lookup → O(n²)
Double coordinates to keep midpoints integral
slides.narration: Checking every group of four points is n to the fourth. Treating each pair as a diagonal and looking up the other two corners in a hash set is quadratic.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Put all points in a hash set
2. For each pair, compute the two remaining corners by rotating around the midpoint
4. Divide by two since each square has two diagonals
slides.narration: Step by step. First, put all points in a hash set. Second, for each pair, compute the two remaining corners by rotating around the midpoint. Third, count when both exist. Fourth, divide by two since each square has two diagonals.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Pick diagonal (1, 1) – (0, 0)
slides.narration: Take (1, 1) and (0, 0) as a diagonal. The midpoint is the square's centre.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Rotate 90° about the midpoint: both corners exist
slides.narration: Rotating the half-diagonal ninety degrees gives the other two corners. Both are in the set, so this is a square.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Answer: 2
slides.narration: We found 8 ordered diagonal pairs. Each square has two diagonals in two orders, so divide by four: 2.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We store doubled coordinates in a set. For each ordered pair, compute the midpoint and the half-diagonal, rotate it to get the other two corners, and count if both exist. Return count over four.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n squared. Space is O of n.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Divide by 4 (each square counted four times)
slides.narration: Each square is counted four times, so divide. Doubling every coordinate keeps midpoints integral, avoiding floating-point keys.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Mention the side-based variant (pairs as edges)
slides.narration: This counts tilted squares too, not just axis-aligned ones. Mention the edge-based variant as an alternative.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Any two points can be a square's diagonal; the other two corners are then fixed, so just check they exist.
slides.narration: To recap Count Squares: Any two points can be a square's diagonal; the other two corners are then fixed, so just check they exist. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
